media_item.item_title: Book Content: Redeeming Justice: From Defendant to Defender, My Fight for Equity on Both Sides of a Broken System
media_item.focus_or_theme: Wrongful conviction, personal memoir, criminal justice reform, racial bias in the justice system
media_item.summary_notes: The book is a personal memoir by Jarrett Adams, recounting his wrongful conviction and subsequent fight for justice.  It details the systemic issues within the American criminal justice system, particularly racial bias, inadequate legal representation, and the challenges faced by exonerees after release. Adams' journey from defendant to defender is highlighted, along with his work to prevent future wrongful convictions.
media_item.case_details_raw: The book details Jarrett Adams' wrongful conviction for sexual assault in Whitewater, Wisconsin in 2000, his nearly 10-year incarceration, and his eventual exoneration in 2007. It also mentions the cases of Dimitri Henley, who was also convicted in the same case, and Richard Beranek, whom Adams later represented.

research_notes_other.post_exoneration_career: After his exoneration, Jarrett Adams earned a law degree from Loyola University Chicago School of Law in 2015, worked with Judge Ann Claire Williams, joined the Innocence Project, co-founded Life After Justice, and established law offices in New York, Chicago, and Milwaukee.

contributing_factors_raw: Perjury/False Accusation: The alleged victim's testimony was contradicted by other witnesses
Inadequate Legal Defense: Defense attorney failed to call a key witness who could have established consent
Racial Bias: Adams and his co-defendants (Black) were tried by an all-white jury for an alleged crime against a white woman
